lead: A monitor makes colour by adding light. A printer makes it by subtracting ink. A person choosing a shade thinks in hue. So one colour needs more than one set of numbers. RGB stores the three lights a screen shows. CMY stores the three inks a printer lays down. HSV re-describes the same RGB triple as hue, saturation and value. Every colour picked in a paint program, web page or phone theme is stored in one model and converted to another before it reaches the device.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for a pixel holding a colour value, and Chapter 1.3 for how that value reaches the screen.

blocks.text: A screen pixel is three tiny lights: red, green and blue. None on gives black; all three full gives white. Colour is made by adding light, so this is additive mixing. Red plus green gives yellow, red plus blue magenta, green plus blue cyan.

Each channel is 8 bits, value 0 to 255. Three channels make 24 bits per pixel, 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 colours, called 24-bit colour or true colour. Shorthand writes the bytes as hex #RRGGBB, so #FF8000 means R = 255, G = 128, B = 0.

Treat R, G and B as three axes from 0 to 1. Every colour sits inside or on the unit cube. Black is (0, 0, 0) at one corner, white (1, 1, 1) at the opposite. The primary corners are red, green and blue; the other three are yellow, cyan and magenta. Grey lies on the diagonal from black to white, where R = G = B.

items: 0 means the light is off, 255 means full brightness.
Equal R, G and B give a grey; 255, 255, 255 is white and 0, 0, 0 is black.
Screens, phones and projectors are RGB devices. Each has its own gamut, the set of colours it can show, and colours outside it are approximated.

sections.h3: CMY and CMYK: colour by subtracting ink

blocks.text: Paper looks white because it reflects light. Ink absorbs some wavelengths and reflects the rest. Cyan ink absorbs red, so the eye sees cyan. Magenta absorbs green; yellow absorbs blue. This is subtractive mixing, and the model is CMY.
CMY is the exact inverse of RGB on the 0 to 1 scale:

blocks.where: R, G and B are red, green and blue on 0 to 1; C, M and Y are cyan, magenta and yellow on the same scale. Multiply by 255 to write bytes.

blocks.text: Printing all three inks on top should give black, but real inks are impure. The mixture is a muddy dark brown, wets the paper and spends three cartridges to darken one spot. Printers add black ink K, giving CMYK. Remove the common part first:
K = min(C, M, Y),   C′ = (C − K) ÷ (1 − K)
blocks.where: K is black ink from 0 to 1; C′ is cyan left after black is removed, and M′ and Y′ are computed the same way. If K = 1 the paper is fully black, so set C′ = M′ = Y′ = 0 and skip the division.

blocks.text: RGB is easy for a machine and awkward for a person. To make orange lighter you must raise R, G and B together and keep their ratios in step. HSV splits the same information into three things people talk about.

items: Hue H is the colour name, an angle in degrees. 0° is red, 60° yellow, 120° green, 180° cyan, 240° blue, 300° magenta, and 360° is red again.
Saturation S is purity, 0 to 1. At S = 0 the colour is grey; at S = 1 it is full strength.
Value V is brightness, 0 to 1. At V = 0 the colour is black, whatever H and S say.

blocks.text: Put greys on a vertical axis and let hue run around it as an angle. You get a hexcone: black at the bottom point, white at the top of the axis, pure hues around the top rim. Any colour is a point inside. A dark muddy red sits low and near the axis; a bright orange sits high and near the rim.
V = max,   S = Δ ÷ max,   H = 60° × (((G − B) ÷ Δ) mod 6) if max is R
blocks.where: R, G and B are scaled to 0 to 1; max and min are the largest and smallest of the three; Δ = max − min. If max is G use 60° × ((B − R) ÷ Δ + 2), and if max is B use 60° × ((R − G) ÷ Δ + 4). If max = 0 set S = 0; if Δ = 0 set H = 0.

items: Divide each byte by 255 to get R, G and B on 0 to 1.
Take V as the largest of the three, and Δ as largest minus smallest.
Divide Δ by V to get S; if V is 0, S is 0.
Find the largest channel, apply its hue formula, and keep H in 0° to 360°.

figure.caption: One colour can be written three ways. The RGB branch adds three lights, the CMY branch subtracts three inks, and the HSV branch names the same colour by hue, saturation and value.

spec.aria: A tree with root Colour models and three branches RGB, CMY and HSV, each with its three components.

examples.question: A framebuffer pixel has 24-bit RGB value (255, 128, 0). Convert to CMY in 0–1 and bytes, then to HSV with hue in degrees, S and V on 0–1. Name the colour.
steps: H = 30.1°, S = 1, V = 1 is bright orange, matching #FF8000.
examples.answer: CMY = (0, 0.498, 1) on 0–1, or (0, 127, 255) as bytes; HSV = (30.1°, 1, 1), a bright orange.
examples.check:
r = 255/255
g = 128/255
b = 0/255
c, m, y = 1-r, 1-g, 1-b
print(round(c, 4), round(m, 4), round(y, 4))
mx, mn = max(r, g, b), min(r, g, b)
d = mx - mn
v = mx
s = 0 if mx == 0 else d/mx
if d == 0:
    h = 0
elif mx == r:
    h = 60*(((g-b)/d) % 6)
elif mx == g:
    h = 60*(((b-r)/d) + 2)
else:
    h = 60*(((r-g)/d) + 4)
print(round(h, 4), round(s, 4), round(v, 4))

traps: CMY is the inverse of RGB, not a reordering: M = 1 − G, never 1 − Y. Forgetting the subtraction shows the model is not understood.
Hue is an angle from 0° to 360°, not a 0–255 channel. Do not divide it by 255 without stating the scale.
S and V differ. V = 1, S = 0 is white; V = 1, S = 1 is a pure hue. Pale pink has high V and low S.
Grey has no hue. When max = min, set H = 0; do not call the division by zero an error in the formula.
Equal C, M, Y do not print black, which is why K exists. When K = 1 the division is undefined, so set C′ = M′ = Y′ = 0.

quiz.q: Name the three RGB components and say what 0 means for each.
quiz.a: Red, green and blue, each 8 bits, 0–255. 0 means that light is off; 255 means full brightness.

quiz.q: A printer can mix cyan, magenta and yellow. Why still add black?
quiz.a: Real inks are impure, so all three give a muddy dark brown, not black. Three inks also wet the paper and cost three cartridges for one dark area. Black ink gives true dark and saves ink, hence CMYK.

quiz.q: Convert RGB (0, 255, 255) to CMY in bytes and HSV with hue in degrees.

quiz.a: Each channel = 64 ÷ 255 = 0.251. max=min=0.251, Δ=0, V=0.251, S=0. Δ=0 makes hue undefined; convention H=0. Dark grey.

quiz.q: Compare RGB (200, 40, 40) and RGB (90, 120, 200) by S and V. Which is more saturated, which brighter?
CMYK printer receives C=0.6, M=0.3, Y=0.6. Find K and C′, M′, Y′.
Why is HSV better than RGB for a colour picker?
quiz.a: A picker offers hue ring, saturation slider and brightness slider, which is how people describe a shade: pale green, dark red. In RGB, changing brightness means moving all three channels together while keeping ratios, which one slider cannot do. HSV makes the three choices independent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production work adds colour management: an ICC profile describes what a monitor or printer does with the numbers, and a conversion engine maps between them so a red on screen survives the trip to paper. HSV is one of a family; HSL is common in web style sheets, and perceptual spaces such as CIELAB and Oklab try to make equal numeric steps look like equal visual steps, which RGB and HSV do not. Video work mostly uses luma plus chroma, so colour is split into brightness and two difference signals before compression.
